newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore boundary changes not electoral ploy - PM.
newsitem.headline: Singapore boundary changes not electoral ploy - PM.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has denied that proposed changes in election rules are aimed at making it harder for opposition candidates to win, the Straits Times newspaper reported on Monday.
It quoted Goh as saying his ruling People's Action Party (PAP) had no plans to use changes in electoral boundaries or multi-member Group Representation Constituencies (GRCs) to defeat the opposition.
"We want to defeat them in a man-to-man fight and that should be done politically, not by absorbing them into GRCs. That is the PAP's preference," he said.
When Goh proposed changes in the GRCs in parliament last week, opposition parties said it would weaken their chances.
Singapore Democratic Party (SDP) assistant secretary-general Kwan Yue Keng called the changes "a series of measures released close to election time, designed to further entrench PAP rule".
Singapore's parliament has 81 elected members, of whom four are currently from the opposition. The island republic must hold a general election by April 1997.
The bills introduced by Goh would raise the maximum number of MPs who can be elected from a multi-member constituency to six, from four.
In these constituencies, votes are cast for slates rather than individual candidates. The slate that wins the most votes takes all of the seats in the constituency.
The proposed changes would also permit a reduction of single-member constituencies to as few as eight from the current 21.
Some opposition leaders said the changes could mean more three-cornered fights in the remaining single-seat wards, splitting the opposition and hurting its chances.
In GRCs, heavyweight PAP ministers could "provide an umbrella for new and possibly weak candidates", National Solidarity Party head Tan Chee Kien said last week.
Singapore's opposition is fragmented into several small parties and the group with three of the four opposition seats, the SDP, has been subject to bitter factional disputes.
